_comment: Department of Basic Education Grade 10 Physical Sciences P1 (Physics), November 2018 national common examination.
Questions and marking-guideline answers extracted from the text layer of the official PDFs
(paper1.pdf, paper1_memo.pdf) and read against the rendered pages. The guideline is
bilingual (English/Afrikaans); only the English is transcribed. memo_answer gives the guideline's
working and final answers (tick marks removed); diagrams, graphs and circuits are described in
brackets in the question text. Data sheets printed with the paper are not transcribed.
FORMAT: 150 marks, 2 hours, eleven compulsory questions (Q1 multiple choice 20 marks). The ANSWER SHEET
(graph paper for QUESTION 3.3) is the last page of paper1.pdf; the graph answers are described in words.

subject: Physical Sciences

questions.context: QUESTION 1: MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS. Various options are provided as possible answers to the following questions. Each question has only ONE correct answer. Choose the answer and write only the letter (A-D) next to the question numbers (1.1 to 1.10) in the ANSWER BOOK, e.g. 1.11 D.
questions.text: An object is positively charged if it has more … A electrons than protons. B electrons than neutrons. C protons than electrons. D protons than neutrons.
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: A car is travelling at a speed of 30 m·s-1 on a straight road. What would be the speed of the car in km∙h-1? A 8,33 km∙h-1 B 30 km∙h-1 C 108 km∙h-1 D 130 km∙h-1
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: The UNIT in which the rate of flow of charge is measured, is called … A ampere. B coulomb. C volt. D watt.
questions.memo_answer: A

questions.text: The gradient of a velocity versus time graph is equivalent to the … A acceleration. B displacement. C position. D total distance covered.
questions.memo_answer: A

questions.text: An object is released from the top of a frictionless inclined plane, AB, as shown below. [Diagram: incline with A at the top and B at the bottom.] Which ONE of the following statements regarding the total mechanical energy of the object is CORRECT? A (Ep + Ek)A > (Ep + Ek)B B (Ep + Ek)A < (Ep + Ek)B C (Ep + Ek)A = (Ep + Ek)B D (Ep + Ek)A = -(Ep + Ek)B
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: Two identical light bulbs are connected in parallel, as shown in the circuit diagram below. Voltmeters V1 and V2 are connected across each light bulb. V1 V2 Which ONE of the following voltmeter readings is CORRECT? A V1 = V2 B V1 = 2V2 C V1 = ½V2 D V1 = ¼V2
questions.memo_answer: A

questions.text: Four identical balloons, each carrying a charge, are suspended from a ceiling, as shown in the diagram below. [Diagram: A and B hang from one rod and pull towards each other until they touch; C and D hang from a second rod, C leans towards B and D leans away from C.] Balloon B is negatively charged. Which combination is CORRECT regarding the charges on the balloons? (SIGN OF CHARGE ON A | ON C | ON D) A - | + | -; B + | + | +; C - | - | -; D + | + | -
questions.memo_answer: B

questions.text: Two cyclists are cycling in opposite directions along the side line of a rectangular field. It is observed that they covered the same distance over a time interval of 3 s. Which ONE of the following physical quantities is the SAME regarding the cyclists over the interval of 3 s? A Acceleration B Average speed C Average velocity D Displacement
questions.memo_answer: B

questions.text: Red light of frequency f and wavelength λ shines on an object. The red light is then replaced by light of a higher energy. How do the frequency and the wavelength of light shining on the object now compare with that of red light? (FREQUENCY | WAVELENGTH) A Greater than f | Remains the same (λ); B Less than f | Greater than λ; C Greater than f | Less than λ; D Remains the same (f) | Less than λ
questions.memo_answer: C

questions.text: Study the following wave patterns: [Four wave traces on identical grids: 1 - three small-amplitude waves across the grid; 2 - four and a half waves of larger amplitude; 3 - two and a half large-amplitude waves; 4 - three larger-amplitude waves.] Which COMBINATION is the CORRECT representation of the wave patterns with the same pitch? A 1 and 2 B 1 and 3 C 1 and 4 D 2 and 4
questions.memo_answer: C/B
questions.memo_note: The guideline accepts either C or B.

questions.context: QUESTION 2 (Start on a new page.) A baby leaves a bowl of food on the floor and crawls westwards to fetch a toy placed 5 m away. At the same time a dog walks eastwards towards the baby. It takes the baby 30 s to reach the toy. The dog walks past the toy to eat the baby's food in the bowl. [Diagram, west to east: dog, 7 m, toy, 5 m, food bowl (where the baby starts).]
questions.text: Define the term displacement in words.
questions.memo_answer:
The difference in position (in space).
OR The change in position (of an object).

questions.text: Determine the position of the dog relative to the baby before they both moved.
questions.memo_answer:
12 m west or -12 m
(If -12 m west: award 1 mark only. Accept 12 m left.)

questions.text: Calculate the average velocity of the baby.
questions.memo_answer:
v = Δx / Δt = 5 / 30 = 0,17 m·s⁻¹ west
(Accept 0,17 m·s⁻¹ left.)

questions.text: If the average speed of the dog is TWICE that of the baby, calculate how long it would take the dog to reach the food bowl from the moment the dog started moving.
questions.memo_answer:
(Positive marking from 2.2 and 2.3.)
Speed of the dog = (0,17)(2) = 0,34 m·s⁻¹
speed = distance / time: 0,34 = 12 / Δt
Δt = 35,29 s

questions.context: QUESTION 3 (Start on a new page.) The diagram below shows the positions of an athlete at different time intervals during a race. [t = 0 s at 0 m (A); 1,5 s at 3 m; 3,0 s at 6 m (B); 4,5 s at 12 m; 6,0 s at 21 m; 7,5 s at 33 m (C).]
questions.text: Distinguish between motion with uniform velocity and uniformly accelerated motion.
questions.memo_answer:
Motion with uniform velocity: motion at constant velocity / motion with zero or no acceleration.
Uniformly accelerated motion: motion with constant acceleration / velocity changes with the same amount during each time interval / motion during which the velocity changes with a constant amount per unit time.

questions.context: 3.2 What type of motion (motion with uniform velocity or uniformly accelerated motion) is represented by the following intervals?
questions.text: A to B
questions.memo_answer: Motion with uniform velocity

questions.text: B to C
questions.memo_answer: Uniformly accelerated motion

questions.text: Use the information in the diagram above to draw an accurate position versus time graph on the graph paper on the attached ANSWER SHEET.
questions.memo_answer:
Position (m) against time (s) graph through (0; 0), (1,5; 3), (3; 6), (4,5; 12), (6; 21), (7,5; 33): a straight line from 0 to 3 s, then a curve getting steeper from 3 s to 7,5 s.
Marking: x-axis and units correctly labelled; y-axis and units correctly labelled; 2 points correctly plotted and joined; shape of the graph 0-3 s straight line; shape of the graph 3-7,5 s curved.

questions.text: Define the term instantaneous velocity in words.
questions.memo_answer:
Instantaneous velocity: rate of change in position.
OR Displacement divided by a very small time interval.
OR Velocity at a particular time.

questions.text: On the graph drawn for QUESTION 3.3, show how you would determine the instantaneous velocity.
questions.memo_answer: Draw a tangent to the curve at the chosen time; its gradient is the instantaneous velocity.

questions.text: Calculate the velocity of the athlete at 3 s.
questions.memo_answer: v = Δx / Δt = (6 - 0) / (3 - 0) = 2 m·s⁻¹ right

questions.context: QUESTION 4 (Start on a new page.) Two cars, A and B, are moving at speeds of 15 m·s⁻¹ and 30 m·s⁻¹ in the same direction. They are side by side when both drivers observe an obstruction ahead of them, as shown in the diagram below. Both drivers apply their brakes and accelerate at -4,5 m·s⁻² until both cars come to rest. Ignore the reaction time of the drivers.
questions.text: Define the term acceleration in words.
questions.memo_answer: The rate of change of velocity.

questions.context: 4.2 Calculate the:
questions.text: Time it takes car A to come to rest
Stopping distance of car A
questions.memo_answer:
OPTION 1: vf² = vi² + 2aΔx: 0² = 15² + 2(-4,5)Δx, Δx = 25 m
OPTION 2 (positive marking from 4.2.1): Δx = ((vf + vi)/2)Δt = ((0 + 15)/2)(3,33) = 24,98 m
OPTION 3 (positive marking from 4.2.1): Δx = viΔt + ½aΔt² = (15)(3,33) + ½(-4,5)(3,33)² = 25 m

questions.text: Which car (A or B) has the longer stopping distance? Support the answer with a calculation.
questions.memo_answer:
OPTION 1: vf² = vi² + 2aΔx: 0² = 30² + 2(-4,5)Δx, Δx = 100 m
Car B has a larger stopping distance (100 m > 25 m).
OPTION 2: vf = vi + aΔt: 0 = 30 + (-4,5)Δt, Δt = 6,67 s; car B takes longer to stop, hence a larger stopping distance.
(If only: car B has a higher velocity than car A and therefore a larger stopping distance at the same acceleration - max 2/6.)

questions.text: What conclusion can be made about the relationship between speed and stopping distance?
questions.memo_answer: The greater the speed, the larger the stopping distance if the acceleration is constant.

questions.context: QUESTION 5 (Start on a new page.) A skateboarder, starting from the top of a ramp 4,5 m above the ground, skates down the ramp, as shown in the diagram below. The mass of the skateboarder and his board is 65 kg. Ignore the effects of friction. [Diagram: ramp from 4,5 m down to point X on the ground, then up to point Y, 6 m above the ground.]
questions.text: Define the term gravitational potential energy in words.
questions.topic: Mechanical energy: kinetic and potential energy
questions.memo_answer: The energy an object has because of its position in the gravitational field relative to some reference point.

questions.text: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the skater just before he skates down the ramp.
questions.topic: Mechanical energy: kinetic and potential energy

questions.text: State the principle of conservation of mechanical energy in words.
questions.memo_answer: The net/total mechanical energy (sum of kinetic and gravitational potential energy) in an isolated/closed system remains constant/is conserved.

questions.text: Use the principle stated in QUESTION 5.3 to calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the skateboarder when he reaches the ground at point X.
Will the skateboarder be able to reach point Y if he were to remain on his skateboard? Write YES or NO and support the answer with a relevant calculation.
questions.memo_answer:
OPTION 1: (Ep + Ek)top = (Ep + Ek)bottom: (65)(9,8)h + 0 = 0 + ½(65)(9,39)²; 637h = 2 865,6; h = 4,49 m
No. h = 4,49 m < 6 m
OPTION 2: Ep at Y = mgh = (65)(9,8)(6) = 3 822 J
Emech < Ep at Y, therefore he will not reach point Y.

questions.context: QUESTION 6 (Start on a new page.) Study the two transverse waves, P and Q, as shown below. [Graph of position (mm) against time (s): wave P (solid) has amplitude 15 mm with crests A and C and troughs B and D; wave Q (dashed) has amplitude 10 mm and the same period; both complete two waves in 3,0 s; the distance from B to D is marked 100 mm.]
questions.text: Write down ONE difference and ONE similarity between wave P and wave Q.
questions.memo_answer:
Difference: amplitudes.
Similarity (any one): wavelength; period; frequency; transverse.

questions.context: 6.2 For wave pattern P, write down:
questions.text: Two points that are out of phase
questions.memo_answer:
A and B
OR C and D
OR B and C
OR A and D

questions.text: The amplitude of the wave
Define the term frequency of the wave in words.
questions.memo_answer: The number of waves/wave pulses passing a point per second.

questions.context: 6.4 For wave pattern Q, calculate the:
questions.text: Frequency of the wave
Speed of the wave
questions.memo_answer:
(Positive marking from 6.4.1.)
OPTION 1: v = fλ = (0,67)(0,1) = 0,067 m·s⁻¹
OPTION 2: v = Δx / Δt = 0,1 / 1,5 = 0,067 m·s⁻¹

questions.context: QUESTION 7 (Start on a new page.) Experiments were done to investigate the effect of temperature on the speed of sound. One person beat a drum while another person, who was standing 50 m away from the sound source, recorded the time travelled by the sound. They performed the experiment at different temperatures at different times of the day. They recorded their findings in the table below. [TEMPERATURE (°C) | TIME (s): 0 | 0,151; 5 | 0,150; 10 | 0,148; 15 | 0,147; 20 | 0,146; 25 | 0,145] 7.1 For the investigation, write down the:
questions.text: Investigative question
questions.memo_answer:
What is the relationship between the speed of sound and temperature?
OR How will the temperature affect the speed of sound?
OR What is the relationship between the time taken for the sound to travel and temperature?
Marking: dependent and independent variables correctly identified; a question about the relationship between the independent and dependent variables.

questions.text: Independent variable
questions.memo_answer: Temperature

questions.text: Dependent variable
questions.memo_answer: Speed of sound / Time taken for the sound to travel.

questions.text: Calculate the speed of sound at 20 °C.
Write down a conclusion for the investigation.
questions.memo_answer: The speed of sound increases / time taken for the sound to travel decreases as the temperature increases.

questions.context: The person who beat the drum noticed that the sound reflected back after a while.
questions.text: Name the term used to describe the reflection of sound waves.
questions.memo_answer: Echo

questions.context: QUESTION 8 (Start on a new page.) The types of electromagnetic radiation are arranged according to frequency in the table below. [Radio waves 10⁵-10¹⁰ Hz; microwaves 10¹⁰-10¹¹ Hz; infrared 10¹¹-10¹⁴ Hz; visible light 10¹⁴-10¹⁵ Hz; ultraviolet 10¹⁵-10¹⁶ Hz; X-rays 10¹⁶-10¹⁸ Hz; gamma rays 10¹⁸-10²¹ Hz]
questions.text: How are electromagnetic waves generated?
questions.memo_answer: Accelerating charges

questions.text: What type of electromagnetic radiation has the highest energy?
questions.memo_answer: Gamma rays

questions.text: Explain the answer to QUESTION 8.2.
questions.memo_answer: It has the highest frequency. Energy is directly proportional to frequency (E ∝ f).

questions.context: 8.4 A certain type of electromagnetic radiation has a wavelength of 600 x 10-10 m.
questions.text: Identify the type of electromagnetic radiation by performing a calculation.
questions.memo_answer:
OPTION 1: c = fλ: 3 x 10⁸ = f(600 x 10⁻¹⁰), f = 5 x 10¹⁵ Hz; ultraviolet
OPTION 2: E = hc / λ = (6,63 x 10⁻³⁴)(3 x 10⁸) / (600 x 10⁻¹⁰) = 3,315 x 10⁻¹⁸ J; E = hf: f = 5 x 10¹⁵ Hz; ultraviolet

questions.text: State ONE application of the type of radiation identified in QUESTION 8.4.1.
questions.memo_answer:
(Positive marking from 8.4.1.)
Any one relevant use: sterilisation of medical equipment; suntan beds; security in currency; astronomy.

questions.context: QUESTION 9 (Start on a new page.) Four metallic bars, suspended freely from a ceiling, interact, as shown in the diagram below. The points of attachment of X and Y on the ceiling are 4 cm apart. [Diagram, left to right: A hangs straight; X (N pole on its left end) and Y lean apart, 5 cm between them; B leans towards Y.] The two bars in the middle are bar magnets (X and Y) and the distance between them is 5 cm. One of the bars (A or B) is made of iron and the other is made of gold.
questions.text: Write down the term describing a material that is easily magnetised.
questions.memo_answer: Ferromagnetic (material)

questions.text: Which ONE of the bars (A or B) is made of iron?
questions.memo_answer: B

questions.text: Determine the polarity of bar B closest to bar magnet Y. Write only NORTH or SOUTH.
questions.memo_answer: South

questions.text: Explain the answer to QUESTION 9.3.
questions.memo_answer:
X (N S) repels Y, so Y is S N (south pole facing X); Y attracts B, so the end of B closest to Y is a south pole.
OR Magnet X repels Y (south pole); magnet Y attracts B (south pole at B).

questions.text: Sketch the magnetic field pattern around bar magnet X.
questions.memo_answer:
Field lines leave the N pole and curve round to enter the S pole of bar magnet X, densest near the poles.
Marking: correct direction of field lines; shape of the magnetic field; no field lines crossing each other.

questions.context: 9.6 Bars A and B are now removed and the points of attachment are now 2 cm, as shown in the diagram below. [X and Y hang from points 2 cm apart.]
questions.text: How will the change in the position of the attachment affect the final distance of separation between the bars? Write only GREATER THAN 5 cm, LESS THAN 5 cm or REMAINS at 5 cm.
questions.memo_answer: Less than 5 cm

questions.text: Explain the answer to QUESTION 9.6.1.
questions.memo_answer:
The magnitude of the magnetic force is inversely proportional to the distance. B is no longer attracting Y to the right.
OR A decrease in distance increases the magnetic force; B is no longer attracting Y to the right.

questions.context: QUESTION 10 (Start on a new page.) Two identical insulated spheres, X and Y, suspended by threads from a ceiling, are held at a small distance apart, as shown in the diagram below. Sphere X carries a charge of +4 x 10⁻¹⁸ C, while sphere Y has an excess of 30 electrons.
questions.text: Calculate the magnitude of the charge on sphere Y.
questions.memo_answer:
n = Q / qe
30 = Q / (-1,6 x 10⁻¹⁹)
Q = -4,8 x 10⁻¹⁸ C
(Accept Q = 4,8 x 10⁻¹⁸ C.)

questions.context: The spheres are now released and they move towards each other.
questions.text: Give a reason why spheres X and Y move towards each other.
questions.memo_answer: Unlike/opposite charges attract.

questions.context: The spheres are allowed to touch each other. After touching, they move away from each other.
questions.text: State the principle of conservation of charge in words.
questions.memo_answer: The net/total charge in an isolated/closed system remains constant/is conserved.

questions.text: Calculate the charge on each sphere after they have separated.
questions.memo_answer:
(Positive marking from 10.1.)
Qnet = (Q1 + Q2) / 2 = (4 x 10⁻¹⁸ + (-4,8 x 10⁻¹⁸)) / 2
= -4 x 10⁻¹⁹ C

questions.context: QUESTION 11 (Start on a new page.) 11.1 Consider the circuit diagram below. [Circuit: 24 V battery with voltmeter V1 across it, ammeter A1, an 8 Ω bulb with voltmeter V2 across it, then a parallel combination of two 8 Ω bulbs, each in series with its own ammeter (A2 and A3), and switch S.] Switch S is OPEN.
questions.text: Write down the reading on the following: (a) Voltmeter (V1) (1) (b) Ammeter (A1) (1)

questions.context: Switch S is now CLOSED.
questions.text: Calculate the equivalent resistance of the circuit.
questions.memo_answer:
OPTION 1: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 = 1/8 + 1/8, Rp = 4 Ω
OPTION 2: Rp = product / sum = (8)(8) / (8 + 8) = 4 Ω
RT = Rs + Rp = 8 + 4 = 12 Ω

questions.text: Calculate the reading on voltmeter V2.
questions.memo_answer:
OPTION 1: V divides in the ratio 8 : 4 (series): V2 = 8/12 x 24 = 2/3 x 24 = 16 V
OPTION 2 (positive marking from 11.1.2): V = IR: 24 = I(12), I = 2 A; V2 = IR = (2)(8) = 16 V

questions.text: How do the readings on ammeters A2 and A3 compare with each other?
questions.memo_answer: A2 = A3

questions.context: 11.2 The graph below shows the relationship between the resistance and the length of the conducting wire. [Graph of resistance (Ω, 0-3,5) against length of wire (mm, 0-70): a straight line through the origin.]
questions.text: Write down the relationship between the resistance and the length of the conducting wire.
questions.memo_answer:
Resistance is directly proportional to the length of the conducting wire.
OR As the length of the wire increases, the resistance increases.

questions.text: Determine the resistance of wire with a length of 30 mm.
questions.memo_answer: 1,35 Ω (range 1,3 Ω to 1,4 Ω)
